urgency.summary: Urgency phishing pressures you to act immediately to avoid a negative outcome.
redFlags: Time pressure like “within 30 minutes” or “final notice”
Threats of account closure or legal action if you don’t comply now
Requests to bypass normal verification or steps
responseSteps: Slow down: don’t click or act while you’re rushed
Verify the message via a trusted channel (known phone number, official portal, or known IT contact)
Look for inconsistencies in sender address and the destination URL
Report it using your organization’s phishing/reporting process

deeperLearning.title: Why urgency works
points: Urgency reduces deliberate thinking and nudges you toward quick “compliance” behavior.
Many phishing campaigns use generic deadlines because they work on a wide audience.
A legitimate organization typically allows time for verification.

intimidation.summary: Intimidation phishing uses fear, shame, or threats to force action and prevent you from questioning the request.
redFlags: Threats of disciplinary action, account lockout, or punitive consequences
Accusatory language (e.g., “we detected wrongdoing”) without evidence
Attempts to move you away from standard verification
responseSteps: Don’t respond in anger or fear—take a moment and breathe
Verify independently using official resources or direct contact
Never enter credentials due to threats
Report the email/message through approved channels

deeperLearning.title: Fear + urgency = reduced scrutiny
points: Intimidation phishing aims to override your normal security instincts.
It often targets specific roles or departments to increase perceived credibility.
Legitimate notices usually provide clear, verifiable context.

scarcity.summary: Scarcity phishing suggests you can benefit only if you act fast because “limited” access or “limited” offers are ending.
redFlags: “Limited time” or “exclusive offer” language tied to a link or form
Rewards or opportunities that require login or sensitive info
Requests that don’t match your organization’s typical process
responseSteps: Treat scarcity claims as a reason to verify, not to click
Check the URL carefully before interacting
Confirm the offer through an official announcement or internal channel
Avoid entering details into unexpected pages

deeperLearning.title: Scarcity changes your decision-making
points: Scarcity messaging can create a sense of missing out (FOMO).
Attackers exploit the desire to “get in now” before others.
If it’s truly legitimate, you should still be able to verify it safely.

authority.summary: Authority phishing leverages perceived power—managers, executives, IT, HR, or vendors—to make you comply.
redFlags: Requests that bypass normal approvals (e.g., “do this without following process”)
Mismatched sender identity vs. claimed authority
Links to pages that don’t belong to the organization being referenced
responseSteps: Challenge the authority: verify with the claimed sender through a separate channel
Follow your organization’s standard verification/approval steps
Never assume a link is safe because it claims to be from leadership or IT

deeperLearning.title: Authority exploits social trust
points: People are more likely to comply when a message appears authoritative.
Phishers often impersonate real roles to reduce resistance.
Security requires independent verification, even for “trusted” senders.

types-of-phishing.summary: Phishing comes in many forms. Attackers may target credentials, payments, systems, or personal information—often by disguising their intent.

deeperLearning.title: A practical way to classify phishing
points: Ask: what are they trying to make you do (click, submit credentials, pay, install, or share data)?
Then ask: what information are they trying to collect, and where would it be sent?
Use that to determine the safest reporting + response path.

types.description: A fake login page or message prompts you to enter a username/password (often for email or VPN).
signals: Spelling/formatting inconsistencies in the page or message
Requests for credentials even when MFA is expected

types.description: Fake invoices or payment requests try to get you to pay a fraudulent vendor or share banking details.
signals: Attachment types or links that don’t match the vendor’s normal pattern
New or changed payment instructions without verification

types.description: Text messages or calls mimic support, banks, or urgent notices to drive clicks, replies, or credential entry.
signals: Short, high-pressure messages with a link or call-back number
Requests for one-time codes (OTP) or account verification over phone
Caller claims unusual activity to force immediate action

types.description: Messages tailored to a person or department to increase credibility and reduce suspicion.
signals: References to internal context, names, or projects (even if fabricated)
Requests that look “role-appropriate” but still violate process
Inconsistent sender details or mismatched domains
